Worked Example: Diamonds

Jonas Wallin

1 Diamonds

In this worked example, we’ll use a beeswarm plot to compare diamond prices across cut grades. The diamonds dataset comes with ggplot2 and contains 53,940 diamonds. It is also used in the course book, ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis by Hadley Wickham, Danielle Navarro, and Thomas Lin Pedersen. See the book’s “Diamonds data” section for an introduction to the dataset.

Let’s load the data and the ggbeeswarm package, which supplies the beeswarm layer.

library(tidyverse)
# install.packages("ggbeeswarm") # if you haven't installed it yet
library(ggbeeswarm)

glimpse(diamonds)
## Rows: 53,940
## Columns: 10
## $ carat   <dbl> 0.23, 0.21, 0.23, 0.29, 0.31, 0.24, 0.24, 0.26, 0.22, 0.23, 0.…
## $ cut     <ord> Ideal, Premium, Good, Premium, Good, Very Good, Very Good, Ver…
## $ color   <ord> E, E, E, I, J, J, I, H, E, H, J, J, F, J, E, E, I, J, J, J, I,…
## $ clarity <ord> SI2, SI1, VS1, VS2, SI2, VVS2, VVS1, SI1, VS2, VS1, SI1, VS1, …
## $ depth   <dbl> 61.5, 59.8, 56.9, 62.4, 63.3, 62.8, 62.3, 61.9, 65.1, 59.4, 64…
## $ table   <dbl> 55, 61, 65, 58, 58, 57, 57, 55, 61, 61, 55, 56, 61, 54, 62, 58…
## $ price   <int> 326, 326, 327, 334, 335, 336, 336, 337, 337, 338, 339, 340, 34…
## $ x       <dbl> 3.95, 3.89, 4.05, 4.20, 4.34, 3.94, 3.95, 4.07, 3.87, 4.00, 4.…
## $ y       <dbl> 3.98, 3.84, 4.07, 4.23, 4.35, 3.96, 3.98, 4.11, 3.78, 4.05, 4.…
## $ z       <dbl> 2.43, 2.31, 2.31, 2.63, 2.75, 2.48, 2.47, 2.53, 2.49, 2.39, 2.…

We will focus on three variables:

  • carat: the diamond’s weight in carats.
  • cut: an ordered cut grade, from Fair to Ideal.
  • price: the price in US dollars.

1.1 Comparing Diamonds of the Same Weight

Large diamonds tend to cost more than small diamonds. To make our comparison more useful, let’s keep only diamonds whose recorded weight is exactly one carat. We include every diamond meeting this condition.

one_carat_diamonds <-
  diamonds %>%
  filter(carat == 1)

nrow(one_carat_diamonds)
## [1] 1558
cut_counts <- count(one_carat_diamonds, cut)
cut_counts
## # A tibble: 5 × 2
##   cut           n
##   <ord>     <int>
## 1 Fair        166
## 2 Good        333
## 3 Very Good   389
## 4 Premium     462
## 5 Ideal       208

This leaves 1,558 diamonds, with between 166 and 462 observations per cut grade. Our question is: How much does price vary among diamonds of the same recorded weight, and how does this differ between cut grades?

2 Beeswarm Plots

In a beeswarm plot, each dot represents one observation. Here, the cut grade determines the group on the horizontal axis, and the dot’s height gives the diamond’s price. Dots are moved sideways to separate observations with similar prices. These horizontal offsets have no numerical meaning, and the prices remain unchanged.

The swarm becomes wider where many observations have similar prices. Its width also depends on the number of observations and the spacing settings, so we include the group counts in the axis labels. size controls the size of the dots, while cex controls the spacing used to arrange them.

Let’s also mark each group’s median using stat_summary(). With fun = median, this layer calculates one median per cut grade. shape = 23 gives us a diamond marker, whose interior we make white with fill = "white".

cut_labels <- paste0(cut_counts$cut, "\n(n = ", cut_counts$n, ")")

ggplot(one_carat_diamonds, aes(cut, price, colour = cut)) +
  geom_beeswarm(size = 1.2, cex = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = median, geom = "point", shape = 23,
    size = 3, fill = "white", colour = "grey20"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("#65549B", "#477AB4", "#209895", "#79AD67", "#DBAF43"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = cut_labels) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "What does a one-carat diamond cost?",
    subtitle = "1,558 diamonds recorded at one carat; every dot is one diamond",
    x = "Cut grade", y = "Price (US dollars)",
    caption = "White diamonds mark group medians."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )

Figure 1: A beeswarm of prices for diamonds recorded at one carat. Each dot represents one diamond, and white markers show group medians.

The plot shows substantial price variation within each grade, including a few diamonds costing more than $15,000. The median price is lowest in the Fair group, but the medians do not increase at every step from Fair to Ideal. Even with recorded weight held fixed, diamond colour and clarity still vary. This comparison therefore describes the observed price distributions; it does not isolate the effect of cut grade on price.

2.1 Try It Yourself

  1. Remove the stat_summary() layer. Which comparisons become harder without the median markers?
  2. Replace geom_beeswarm(size = 1.2, cex = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) with geom_violin(). What does the violin summarize, and what information about individual diamonds becomes harder to see?
  3. Return to the beeswarm and try different values of size and cex. How do these choices affect your ability to see individual diamonds and the overall distribution?
